article.title: Democracy Strikes Back
article.author: John Peeler
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. I owe Judy Peeler thanks for inspiring this comparison. October 5, 1988: Dictator General Augusto Pinochet is unexpectedly and overwhelmingly defeated in a referendum intended to authorize a second eight-year term as President. After his efforts to hold on to power are blocked by other members of the military junta, Pinochet follows his own rules and stages a general election in 1989 that ends his 16 year dictatorship and restores democracy in Chile after the violent coup that overthrew the last elected president, Salvador Allende, in 1973. April 12, 2026: After a decade in power, Prime Minister Victor Orbán is unexpectedly defeated in a parliamentary election. His previously dominant party is almost wiped out as a parliamentary presence. Peter Magyar, the new prime minister, swiftly erases the authoritarian measures designed to keep Orbán in power, and restores Hungarian democracy. Orbán pioneered techniques of “electoral authoritarianism” designed to retain the trappings of electoral democracy while making opposition victory all but impossible. November 3, 2026: Just two years after the election that returned him to office, President Donald Trump is overwhelmingly rejected in the midterm elections for Congress, state legislatures and governors. In his final two years as President, Trump will face a strongly Democratic House and Senate that will investigate the misdeeds of his regime, check his misuse of funds, and lay the groundwork for a probable Democratic President in 2028. Trump had patterned his electoral authoritarianism on that of Orban. Related: Trump's Political Collapse Was Entirely His Own Making After a generation of democracy in retreat around the world, and ten years when Trump’s right-wing authoritarianism has dominated politics in the United States, we are seeing a resurgence of democracy as evidenced in the defeats this year of Orbán and Trump. The defeat of Pinochet 38 years ago prefigured this resurgence. Indeed, it was in its time a key part of the resurgence of democracy all over Latin America after of decade of brutal right-wing dictatorships that were promoted and protected by the United States. In all three cases the regime was defeated, not by violent uprisings, but by the people’s vote. This was not entirely surprising in the US and Hungarian cases, since both regimes retained the trappings of electoral democracy. But Pinochet was a straight-up military dictator who had ordered the executions and disappearances of thousands of people. Yet even he felt, eventually, constrained to clothe his regime in the legitimacy of the popular vote. He did this by getting popular endorsement of a constitution that would let him rule for eight years, then have a referendum to confirm him in a second eight year term. He obviously assumed that he would prevail in that referendum, hence failed to fix the election. Big mistake. Related: Receivership: Agenda for a Democratic Congress In the last century, democracy has emerged worldwide as the only widely accepted principle of political legitimacy. There are still regimes that defy that principle, including Saudi Arabia and China, but most dictatorships try to clothe themselves in popular consent, even if that consent is coerced. Russia is a prime example. So is Iran. Other legitimacy principles, such as hereditary or religious authority, are just not believed by many people anymore. Without the trappings of popular consent, Pinochet was an emperor with no clothes. Similarly, Orbán and Trump, for all their authoritarian aspirations, had to keep elections, and couldn’t go too far in fixing the outcomes without undermining their legitimacy. Electoral authoritarianism is the attempt to dictate within democracy. Finally, democracy trumped Trump. The crisis of democracy is by no means over. Electoral authoritarians are still entrenched in Russia, Turkey and India, and far-right parties are surging in France and Germany. And it is deeply problematic when only one party defends democracy, as in Brazil and the United States. In the long term, democracy can only thrive when alternation of parties in power does not threaten democracy itself. Still, we are right to celebrate these victories for democracy against the spirit of darkness and division.
